query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In a multi‐phase eutectic high-entropy alloy, mechanical wear at elevated temperature preferentially damages the protective oxide/passivation layers at phase boundaries, which intensifies micro‐galvanic corrosion between electrochemically dissimilar phases. This synergistic coupling accelerates both the wear and corrosion degradation compared to a uniform, single‐phase counterpart.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy featuring at least two distinct phases with different electrochemical characteristics and naturally forming protective oxide layers on the more noble phase.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to simultaneous mechanical wear (e.g., reciprocating sliding) and corrosive exposure at elevated temperature.
generation.conditions: Elevated operating temperatures (e.g., 450–650 °C or higher, as relevant) in a corrosive environment (such as molten salt or acidic media) with applied mechanical stress producing wear.
generation.structural_mediator: Phase boundaries between the dissimilar phases that result in a micro-galvanic couple, and the integrity of the surface oxide/passivation layer.
generation.mechanism: Wear mechanically disrupts the protective surface oxide at phase interfaces. This exposes the underlying, less noble phase to accelerated anodic dissolution due to micro-galvanic differences. The ongoing wear continuously renews sites of corrosion, thereby establishing a feedback loop that accelerates both wear damage (via increased surface roughness and debris generation) and corrosion (via enhanced chemical attack) in a coupled manner.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline alloy that is single-phase or with more homogenous passivation, the multi-phase eutectic alloy is expected to show a higher total degradation rate with both an increased wear loss and higher corrosion rate. The synergy between wear and corrosion should manifest as greater localized material loss and surface damage than the sum of individual effects.
generation.baseline: A compositionally similar single-phase high-entropy alloy or a multi-phase alloy in which the phase boundaries have been engineered to minimize galvanic potential differences, tested under identical temperature, corrosive, and mechanical wear conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conditions where the temperature is sufficiently high to promote both active corrosion kinetics and wear-induced oxide disruption, in corrosive media that support galvanic activity, and when mechanical stresses are severe enough to disturb the passivation layer.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative increases in wear and corrosion rates remain uncertain without empirical calibration; the strength of the coupling effect may depend on the specific phase chemistries and microstructural scale. Additional work is needed to determine the threshold conditions for the transition from protective to deleterious oxide behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a controlled experiment where two sets of specimens are prepared: one being the multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy and the other a matched single-phase alloy (or an alloy engineered to minimize galvanic couple effects) with similar overall composition. Expose both sets to identical elevated temperature conditions under simultaneous wear (e.g., using reciprocating sliding wear apparatus) and corrosive attack (e.g., molten salt or acidic environment). Measure mass loss, wear track morphology, and electrochemical parameters over time.
measurements: Wear track depth and morphology (via profilometry or microscopy)
Electrochemical measurements (e.g., corrosion potential, current density)
Surface analysis to assess oxide integrity (using XPS or SEM-EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multi-phase eutectic alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in combined degradation (indicated by either similar or lower total mass loss, wear, and corrosion rates, or without evidence of localized micro-galvanic attack at phase boundaries) compared to the single-phase baseline under identical test conditions, then the proposed wear-induced micro-galvanic corrosion mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
